title: Undoer of knots
hook: a painting in Augsburg shows Mary untying a knotted ribbon, and the devotion travels with Pope Francis

segments.voice: Yesterday, the new Eve: Irenaeus and the knot that Mary's yes untied. Your line was the knot untied. Which loop did you loosen? Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

Above an altar in a church in Augsburg, in Germany, hangs a painting. Mary stands in the middle, with angels around her. On one side, an angel hands her a long white ribbon full of knots. Her hands are busy, working one of them loose. On the other side, another angel carries the ribbon away, smooth. That's the whole drama of the picture: a woman patiently untying knots. Yesterday's line from Irenaeus has a face. Today's word: undoer of knots.
screen: `A PAINTING IN AUGSBURG.` → `A RIBBON FULL OF KNOTS.` → `HANDS AT WORK.`

segments.voice: First, the idea behind the picture. Tradition links it to Irenaeus's knot: what Eve's disobedience tied, Mary's obedience loosened. Read that way, the canvas gives an ancient bishop's sentence a ribbon and a pair of hands. Second, what the knots came to mean. In the devotion that grew around the painting, the knots are the tangles of a life: a marriage in trouble, a family that won't speak, a habit that won't let go, a fear wound so tight there's no loose end to pull. People bring their particular knot to Mary and ask her to pray for them, with God's grace, to work it loose. Third, how it traveled. The story goes that a young Jesuit from Argentina, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, came across the image while studying in Germany. Back in Buenos Aires, he gave out cards with the picture, and a devotion took root there. He later became Pope Francis. Fourth, the patience in it. Look at Mary's hands in the painting. She isn't slashing the ribbon with a knife. A knot pulled hard gets tighter. A knot worked slowly, a little this way and a little that, gives. That's one picture of how grace can work: not all at once, but loop by loop. In Catholic teaching Mary doesn't replace God here. She prays, as a mother would, and God does the untying through her prayer. And the picture is simple to carry: a tangle, a pair of patient hands, and a ribbon coming free.
screen: `IRENAEUS'S KNOT, PAINTED.` · `THE KNOTS OF A LIFE.` · `FROM GERMANY TO BUENOS AIRES.` · `NOT CUT: WORKED LOOSE.` · then, large: `SHE UNDOES KNOTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring one knot to prayer. Settle, and breathe. Let one knot in your life come to mind. Not every knot, just one. Look at it honestly. Where's it tight? What keeps pulling it tighter? Now imagine handing that knotted stretch of ribbon to someone with patient hands. You don't have to see how it comes undone. If you pray, you can ask Mary, undoer of knots, to pray for you, using the words of the Hail Mary. If you don't, simply rest, and loosen your grip a little. The bell holds the time.

Undoer of knots. A title for Mary from a painting in Augsburg. And this week's road: the cost is the point, conscience at the checkout, love made structural, four teachings, ever virgin, the knot untied, and now she undoes knots. Today's word.
Your line: she undoes knots. Today, when something tangles, slow your hands down. Loosen it loop by loop instead of pulling hard. Day one thousand three hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Catholics who keep this devotion pray before copies of the Augsburg image, often with the rosary or a novena, naming a particular trouble.
